headline: How Your Click Becomes a Webpage
tldr: A plain-English map of everything that happens between your Wi-Fi signal and the website loading on screen.
summary: The internet is presented as a massive, collaboratively-run network of computers with no single owner, held together by shared standards. Every device — phone, laptop, smart TV — reaches it through a local network, usually home Wi-Fi or a cellular connection, with a router acting as the traffic manager that hands requests off to your internet service provider.

Every device gets a unique IP address (IPv4 or IPv6) so data knows where to go, and that data never travels as one piece — it's chopped into packets that can take different routes and get reassembled at the destination. Those packets ride the internet's backbone: high-speed fiber and undersea cables linking cities and continents, maintained in part by ISPs who provide your connection and IP address.

Typing a web address triggers DNS, described as the internet's phone book, which translates that human-readable domain into a numerical IP address in milliseconds. Your device then contacts the actual web server, which sends back the site's files, and your browser turns that raw data into a page using HTML for structure, CSS for style, and JavaScript for interactivity.

Security threads through the whole system: HTTPS encrypts the browser-to-server connection, firewalls filter traffic, VPNs hide your IP and encrypt your data, and the video flags malware and phishing as the everyday risks to watch for. It also runs through the internet's daily-use layer — email, buffered video streaming, cloud storage, social media, e-commerce, and search — all riding the same infrastructure.

Underneath it all sit protocols like TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP and SMTP that let different systems talk to each other, plus concepts like bandwidth and latency that shape how fast things feel. The video closes on governance and the future: net neutrality, oversight bodies like ICANN, IETF and W3C, and next-wave tech like 5G, AI and quantum computing.
mindmap:
# How the Internet Works

## Getting Online
- Devices connect via Wi-Fi or cellular
- Wi-Fi uses radio waves to reach router
- Router assigns local IP addresses
- Router forwards requests to ISP

## Addressing and Data Transport
- IP addresses uniquely identify devices
  - IPv4 most common
  - IPv6 growing with more devices
- Data split into packets
  - Packets can take different routes
  - Reassembled at the destination
- Internet backbone links countries
  - Undersea cables and fiber optic lines
- ISPs provide the connection
  - Maintain infrastructure, manage traffic

## From Domain to Webpage
- Domain names map to IP addresses
- DNS translates names to addresses
  - Called the internet's phone book
- Browser sends request to web server
- Server responds with site files

## Building the Page
- HTML structures content
- CSS controls look and feel
- JavaScript adds interactivity
- Browser renders it all together

## Staying Secure
- HTTPS encrypts browser-server traffic
- Firewalls block unauthorized access
- VPNs hide IP, encrypt data
- Malware and phishing are named threats

## Everyday Internet Services
- Email routes through mail servers
- Streaming buffers video in chunks
- Cloud computing stores data remotely
- Social media relies on huge server infrastructure
- E-commerce secures payments and data
- Search engines index the web
- IoT connects everyday objects

## Rules and Oversight
- Protocols like HTTP, FTP, SMTP set standards
- TCP/IP is the core communication protocol
- Net neutrality treats all traffic equally
- ICANN, IETF, W3C set web standards

stickies.text: The internet is a massive network of computers and devices that communicate with each other.
Your data doesn't travel in one big chunk — it's broken into packets that take different routes.
Undersea cables link continents while fiber optic lines move data at the speed of light.
DNS acts like the internet's phone book, translating domain names into IP addresses.
The DNS lookup happens in milliseconds, making web browsing feel instant.
Always look for the padlock icon in your browser to ensure a secure connection.
Cookies make browsing convenient but can also be used for tracking and advertising.
Phishing is a trick where attackers pretend to be trustworthy to steal your data.
Staying safe online means keeping devices updated and being cautious with suspicious links.

receipts.title: Wi-Fi and Routers Get You Online
receipts.detail: Wi-Fi uses radio waves to link your device to a router, which assigns local IP addresses and forwards requests to your ISP.

receipts.title: IP Addresses Identify Every Device
receipts.detail: Every device has a unique IP address, either IPv4 or IPv6, acting like a home address so data reaches the right place.

receipts.title: Data Travels as Small Packets
receipts.detail: Messages and web pages are split into packets that can take different paths across the network and are reassembled at the destination.

receipts.title: The Backbone and ISPs Move Data
receipts.detail: High-speed cables, undersea links, and fiber optics form the internet's backbone, while ISPs maintain infrastructure and hand out IP addresses.

receipts.title: DNS Translates Names to Addresses
receipts.detail: DNS servers convert human-friendly domain names into numerical IP addresses in milliseconds, described as the internet's phone book.

receipts.title: Browsers Request Pages From Web Servers
receipts.detail: Once the IP address is known, a request travels through your network, ISP, and the backbone to a web server, which sends back the site's files.

receipts.title: HTML and CSS Build the Page
receipts.detail: HTML structures content like headings, paragraphs and links, while CSS controls colors, fonts and layout to make pages visually appealing.

receipts.title: JavaScript Makes Pages Interactive
receipts.detail: JavaScript runs in the browser to add animations, popups and dynamic behavior whenever you click a button or interact with a page.

receipts.title: HTTPS and Firewalls Keep You Safe
receipts.detail: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server to stop hackers intercepting passwords or card numbers, while firewalls filter incoming and outgoing traffic.

receipts.title: VPNs Encrypt Data and Hide Location
receipts.detail: A VPN creates a secure tunnel that encrypts your data, hides your IP address, and can let you access region-restricted content.

receipts.title: TCP/IP Delivers Data Reliably
receipts.detail: TCP breaks data into packets and ensures correct delivery while IP handles addressing and routing, together forming the internet's core protocol.

receipts.title: Standards Bodies Govern the Internet
receipts.detail: Groups like ICANN, IETF, and W3C set the rules for domain names, protocols, and web standards to keep the internet open and interoperable.

moves: Check for the padlock/HTTPS icon before entering passwords or card details on any site
Look up whether your home network uses IPv4 or IPv6 in your router settings
Turn on two-factor authentication for your most important online accounts
Review and clear unnecessary cookies in your browser's privacy settings
Try a VPN and compare your visible IP address and location before and after

cards.q: What are the two main types of IP address?
cards.a: IPv4 and IPv6; IPv4 is most common, but IPv6 is growing as more devices connect.

cards.q: How does data actually travel across the internet?
cards.a: It's broken into smaller packets that can take different routes and are reassembled at the destination.

cards.q: What does DNS do when you type a web address?
cards.a: It translates the human-readable domain name into a machine-readable IP address, acting like an internet phone book.

cards.q: What are the separate jobs of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript?
cards.a: HTML structures content, CSS controls look and layout, and JavaScript adds interactivity and animation.
